Water:
# Water
## Structure and hydrogen bonding
Water is a polar molecule because oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends are slightly positive. A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen atom of one molecule and a slightly negative atom of another. Hydrogen bonds between water molecules explain most of water's unusual properties.

## Properties of water
Cohesion is the attraction between water molecules caused by hydrogen bonding. Cohesion lets water be pulled up xylem vessels in a continuous column and gives water surface tension. Adhesion is the attraction between water molecules and other polar surfaces, such as cellulose in cell walls, which helps capillary action.
Water is a solvent for polar and ionic substances because its partial charges surround and separate ions and polar molecules. Hydrophilic substances dissolve in or are attracted to water; hydrophobic substances, such as lipids, are not.
Water has a high specific heat capacity, so a lot of energy is needed to change its temperature, which keeps habitats and body temperatures stable. Water has a high latent heat of vaporization, so evaporating sweat removes a lot of heat and cools the body.

## Water and life
Life is thought to have originated in water. The physical properties of water, such as buoyancy, viscosity and thermal conductivity, affect the animals living in it, for example ringed seals and black-throated loons. Water may have reached Earth from asteroids, and the search for life elsewhere focuses on planets that can hold liquid water, in the so-called Goldilocks zone.

## Key terms
Polarity: an uneven distribution of charge across a molecule
Hydrogen bond: a weak attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen atom and a slightly negative atom of another molecule
Cohesion: attraction between molecules of the same substance
Adhesion: attraction between molecules of different substances
Specific heat capacity: the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C
Hydrophobic: not attracted to water
Nucleic acids:
# Nucleic acids
## Structure of DNA and RNA
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the genetic material of all living organisms. A nucleotide is the monomer of nucleic acids, made of a phosphate group, a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base. In DNA the sugar is deoxyribose; in RNA it is ribose.
The bases in DNA are adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine; RNA has uracil instead of thymine. Nucleotides join by covalent bonds between the phosphate of one and the sugar of the next, forming a sugar–phosphate backbone.
DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine pairs with guanine. RNA is usually a single strand.

## Information and the genetic code
The sequence of bases stores genetic information, and the number of possible sequences is almost limitless. The genetic code is universal: the same codons code for the same amino acids in almost all organisms, which is evidence of common ancestry.

## Higher level: structure and evidence
Purines (adenine and guanine) have two rings and pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine and uracil) have one, so every base pair has one of each and the helix has a constant width. In eukaryotes DNA is wound round histone proteins to form nucleosomes, which pack it into chromosomes. The Hershey–Chase experiment showed that DNA, not protein, is the genetic material of viruses. Chargaff found that in DNA the amount of adenine equals thymine and the amount of cytosine equals guanine.

## Key terms
Nucleotide: a monomer made of a phosphate, a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base
Complementary base pairing: the pairing of adenine with thymine (or uracil) and cytosine with guanine
Antiparallel: running in opposite directions
Purine: a two-ring base: adenine or guanine
Pyrimidine: a one-ring base: cytosine, thymine or uracil
Nucleosome: a unit of DNA wound round a core of histone proteins
Origins of cells:
# Origins of cells
## Conditions on the early Earth
The origin of cells is thought to have needed the abiotic synthesis of simple organic molecules, their assembly into polymers, the formation of membranes, and a molecule able to replicate itself. The Miller–Urey experiment showed that amino acids can form from methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour with electric sparks, imitating the early atmosphere.

## RNA world and membranes
The RNA world hypothesis proposes that RNA was the first genetic material, because RNA can both store information and act as a catalyst; a catalytic RNA is called a ribozyme. Fatty acids can form vesicles spontaneously in water, which may have been the first membranes enclosing a separate internal environment.

## LUCA
LUCA (the last universal common ancestor) is the most recent organism from which all life on Earth is descended. Evidence for LUCA comes from the universal genetic code and from genes shared by all organisms. LUCA probably lived near hydrothermal vents around 4 billion years ago.

## Key terms
Abiogenesis: the origin of life from non-living matter
Ribozyme: an RNA molecule that acts as a catalyst
RNA world hypothesis: the idea that RNA was the first genetic material and catalyst
LUCA: the last universal common ancestor of all life on Earth
Vesicle: a small sac enclosed by a membrane
Cell structure:
# Cell structure
## Cell theory and microscopy
Cell theory states that cells are the basic unit of life, all living organisms are made of cells, and cells come only from pre-existing cells. Magnification is how many times larger an image is than the actual object. Resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points as separate. Electron microscopes have a much higher resolution than light microscopes, so they show organelles in detail.

## Structures common to all cells
All cells have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA and ribosomes. The plasma membrane is the boundary that controls what enters and leaves the cell. Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis.

## Prokaryotes and eukaryotes
A prokaryote is a cell without a nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; its DNA is a single circular chromosome in the nucleoid, and it has 70S ribosomes. Many prokaryotes also have a cell wall, plasmids, pili and flagella. A eukaryote is a cell with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus; it has 80S ribosomes.
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole. Animal cells have no cell wall and only small temporary vacuoles. Fungal cells have a cell wall made of chitin.

## Atypical cells
Some cells do not fit the usual pattern: red blood cells have no nucleus, skeletal muscle fibres have many nuclei, aseptate fungal hyphae are not divided into cells, and phloem sieve tube elements have no nucleus.

## Key terms
Cell theory: the theory that all organisms are made of cells, cells are the basic unit of life and cells come from pre-existing cells
Magnification: how many times larger an image is than the real object
Resolution: the ability to distinguish two close points as separate
Prokaryote: a cell without a nucleus or membrane-bound organelles
Eukaryote: a cell with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
Plasmid: a small circle of DNA found in many prokaryotes
Nucleoid: the region of a prokaryote containing its DNA
Viruses:
# Viruses
## What viruses are
A virus is a non-living infectious particle made of genetic material inside a protein coat called a capsid. Viruses have no cytoplasm, carry out no metabolism and can only reproduce inside a host cell. Their genetic material can be DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded. Some viruses also have a lipid envelope taken from the host cell membrane.

## Viral replication
The lytic cycle is the replication cycle in which a virus takes over the host cell, makes many copies of itself and then bursts the cell. The lysogenic cycle is a cycle in which the viral DNA is inserted into the host chromosome and copied with it, becoming active later. Bacteriophage lambda can follow either cycle.

## Origins and evolution of viruses
Viruses are diverse and probably evolved more than once. Viruses evolve rapidly because they have short generation times and high mutation rates, especially RNA viruses. Rapid evolution of HIV and influenza makes vaccines and treatments less effective over time.

## Key terms
Capsid: the protein coat of a virus
Lytic cycle: viral replication that ends with the host cell bursting
Lysogenic cycle: viral replication in which viral DNA is inserted into the host chromosome
Bacteriophage: a virus that infects bacteria
Envelope: a lipid membrane around some viruses taken from the host
Diversity of organisms:
# Diversity of organisms
## Species
A species is a group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. The biological species concept is hard to apply to organisms that reproduce asexually, to fossils and to hybrids. A binomial is the two-part scientific name of a species: the genus and the species, for example Homo sapiens.

## Variation and chromosomes
Members of a species vary, but less than members of different species. A karyotype is an image of all the chromosomes of a cell arranged in pairs by size and banding pattern. Chromosome number is a characteristic of a species: humans have 46 chromosomes and chimpanzees have 48.

## Genomes and identification
A genome is the whole of the genetic information of an organism. Genome size varies between species and is not closely linked to complexity. A dichotomous key is a series of paired choices used to identify organisms. DNA barcoding identifies species by sequencing a short standard section of DNA.

## Key terms
Species: a group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
Binomial nomenclature: naming a species by its genus and species
Karyotype: an image of all the chromosomes of a cell in pairs
Genome: all the genetic information of an organism
Dichotomous key: a series of paired choices used to identify organisms
Classification and cladistics:
# Classification and cladistics
## Classification
Classification is the arrangement of organisms into groups. The traditional hierarchy of taxa is domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. Life is divided into three domains, Archaea, Eubacteria and Eukaryota, based on evidence such as ribosomal RNA sequences.

## Cladistics
A clade is a group made of a common ancestor and all of its descendants. A cladogram is a tree diagram showing the most likely sequence of divergence in a clade. A node is a branching point on a cladogram that represents a common ancestor. Cladograms are based on shared derived characteristics, increasingly from DNA and protein sequences.
The molecular clock is the idea that differences in sequences build up at a roughly constant rate, so the number of differences indicates the time since two groups diverged. Parsimony analysis chooses the cladogram that needs the fewest changes.

## Reclassification
Cladistic evidence has led to reclassification; for example, the figwort family was split after DNA evidence showed it was not a single clade.

## Key terms
Clade: a common ancestor and all its descendants
Cladogram: a tree diagram showing the most likely order of divergence
Node: a branch point on a cladogram representing a common ancestor
Molecular clock: using the rate of sequence change to estimate time since divergence
Domain: the highest taxonomic rank: Archaea, Eubacteria or Eukaryota
Evolution and speciation:
# Evolution and speciation
## Evidence for evolution
Evolution is a change in the heritable characteristics of a population over time. Evidence for evolution comes from fossils, selective breeding, homologous structures and DNA and protein sequences. Homologous structures are structures with the same basic plan in different species, inherited from a common ancestor, such as the pentadactyl limb. Analogous structures have the same function but different origins, the result of convergent evolution.

## Speciation
Speciation is the formation of a new species by the splitting of an existing one. Reproductive isolation is needed for speciation. Allopatric speciation happens when populations are separated geographically. Sympatric speciation happens in the same area, for example through behavioural or temporal isolation. Polyploidy, having more than two sets of chromosomes, can cause rapid sympatric speciation in plants.

## Patterns of evolution
Adaptive radiation is the rapid evolution of many species from one ancestor into different niches, as in Darwin's finches. Hybridization between species often produces sterile offspring, such as the mule, which prevents gene flow between them.

## Key terms
Evolution: change in the heritable characteristics of a population over time
Homologous structures: structures with the same basic plan inherited from a common ancestor
Convergent evolution: unrelated species evolving similar features
Speciation: the formation of new species
Allopatric speciation: speciation after geographical separation
Sympatric speciation: speciation without geographical separation
Polyploidy: having more than two sets of chromosomes
Adaptive radiation: rapid evolution of many species from one ancestor into different niches
Conservation of biodiversity:
# Conservation of biodiversity
## Biodiversity
Biodiversity is the variety of life in all its forms, including genetic, species and ecosystem diversity. Current extinction rates are far higher than background rates, so many scientists describe a sixth mass extinction.

## Causes of biodiversity loss
The main causes of biodiversity loss are habitat destruction, overexploitation, pollution, invasive species and climate change, all increased by human population growth. Extinctions caused by humans include the North Island giant moa, the Caribbean monk seal and the Abingdon Island giant tortoise.

## Conservation
In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitats, such as in nature reserves. Ex situ conservation protects species outside their habitats, in zoos, botanic gardens and seed banks. Rewilding restores ecosystems by reintroducing species and reducing human management. The EDGE of Existence programme prioritises species that are evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered.

## Key terms
Biodiversity: the variety of life, including genetic, species and ecosystem diversity
In situ conservation: protecting species in their natural habitat
Ex situ conservation: protecting species outside their natural habitat
Rewilding: restoring ecosystems by reintroducing species and reducing management
Invasive species: a non-native species that spreads and harms its new ecosystem
Carbohydrates and lipids:
# Carbohydrates and lipids
## Carbon compounds
Carbon can form four covalent bonds, which allows a huge variety of stable molecules. A condensation reaction joins two molecules and releases water. A hydrolysis reaction breaks a bond by adding water.

## Carbohydrates
A monosaccharide is a single sugar unit, such as glucose, fructose or ribose. A disaccharide is two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond, such as maltose, sucrose or lactose. A polysaccharide is a long chain of monosaccharides.
Starch is the energy store of plants and is made of amylose and amylopectin. Glycogen is the energy store of animals and is highly branched. Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide of beta-glucose in plant cell walls; its chains form strong microfibrils. Glycoproteins are proteins with carbohydrate chains that act in cell recognition, such as the ABO blood group antigens.

## Lipids
Lipids are hydrophobic molecules that dissolve in non-polar solvents. A triglyceride is made of one glycerol and three fatty acids joined by ester bonds. Saturated fatty acids have no carbon–carbon double bonds; unsaturated fatty acids have one or more, which bend the chain and lower the melting point. Phospholipids have a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic tails, so they form bilayers. Steroids, such as cholesterol and oestradiol, have four fused rings. Lipids store energy more compactly than carbohydrates and give thermal insulation.

## Key terms
Monosaccharide: a single sugar unit
Glycosidic bond: the bond joining two monosaccharides
Condensation: a reaction that joins molecules and releases water
Hydrolysis: a reaction that breaks a bond by adding water
Triglyceride: a lipid made of glycerol and three fatty acids
Phospholipid: a lipid with a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails
Unsaturated fatty acid: a fatty acid with at least one carbon–carbon double bond
Proteins:
# Proteins
## Amino acids
An amino acid is the monomer of proteins, with an amine group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group. There are 20 amino acids in proteins coded by the genetic code. Amino acids join by condensation to form a peptide bond. A polypeptide is a chain of amino acids. Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body and must come from the diet.

## Protein structure
The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids. The secondary structure is the folding of the chain into alpha helices or beta-pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions. The quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more polypeptides, as in haemoglobin.
Denaturation is a change in a protein's three-dimensional shape, caused by heat or extreme pH, that stops it working.

## Fibrous and globular proteins
Fibrous proteins, such as collagen, are long, insoluble and structural. Globular proteins, such as insulin and haemoglobin, are compact, soluble and functional. The function of a protein depends on its shape.

## Key terms
Peptide bond: the bond between two amino acids
Primary structure: the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide
Tertiary structure: the three-dimensional folding of a polypeptide
Quaternary structure: the association of two or more polypeptides
Denaturation: a change in protein shape that stops it working
Essential amino acid: an amino acid that must come from the diet
Membranes and membrane transport:
# Membranes and membrane transport
## Membrane structure
The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane as a phospholipid bilayer with proteins moving within it. Integral proteins are embedded in the bilayer; peripheral proteins are attached to its surface. Cholesterol in animal membranes regulates fluidity. Glycoproteins and glycolipids on the outer surface are involved in cell recognition.

## Passive transport
Simple diffusion is the net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration. Facilitated diffusion is diffusion through channel or carrier proteins. Osmosis is the net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration. Aquaporins are channel proteins that let water cross membranes quickly.

## Active and bulk transport
Active transport is the movement of particles against a concentration gradient using energy from ATP and pump proteins, such as the sodium–potassium pump. Endocytosis is the taking in of material by the membrane folding inwards to form a vesicle. Exocytosis is the release of material when a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane. Gated ion channels open in response to a signal, such as a neurotransmitter or a change in voltage.

## Key terms
Fluid mosaic model: a phospholipid bilayer with proteins moving within it
Simple diffusion: net movement of particles down a concentration gradient
Facilitated diffusion: diffusion through channel or carrier proteins
Osmosis: net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane to a higher solute concentration
Active transport: movement against a concentration gradient using ATP
Endocytosis: taking material in by the membrane folding inwards
Exocytosis: releasing material as a vesicle fuses with the membrane
Aquaporin: a channel protein for water
Organelles and compartmentalization:
# Organelles and compartmentalization
## Compartmentalization
Compartmentalization is the division of a eukaryotic cell into membrane-bound organelles, which separates incompatible processes and concentrates enzymes and substrates. The nuclear membrane separates transcription in the nucleus from translation in the cytoplasm.

## Organelles
The nucleus contains the chromosomes and has a double membrane with pores. The rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes and makes proteins for secretion. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles. Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes. Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration and have a double membrane with folded cristae. Chloroplasts are the site of photosynthesis and contain stacks of thylakoids called grana.

## Endosymbiosis
The endosymbiotic theory states that mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from prokaryotes taken in by an ancestral eukaryote. Evidence includes their double membranes, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and division by binary fission.

## Cell fractionation
Cell fractionation is the separation of organelles by breaking cells open and spinning the mixture in a centrifuge, so that heavier organelles settle out first.

## Key terms
Compartmentalization: dividing a cell into membrane-bound organelles
Rough endoplasmic reticulum: membranes with ribosomes that make proteins for secretion
Golgi apparatus: the organelle that modifies, sorts and packages proteins
Lysosome: a vesicle containing digestive enzymes
Mitochondrion: the site of aerobic respiration
Chloroplast: the site of photosynthesis
Endosymbiotic theory: the theory that mitochondria and chloroplasts came from engulfed prokaryotes
Cell specialization:
# Cell specialization
## Differentiation
A zygote is the cell formed when two gametes fuse; it divides to form an embryo. Differentiation is the process by which cells become specialized for a particular function by expressing some genes and not others. Gradients of morphogens in the embryo signal which genes each cell should express.

## Stem cells
A stem cell is an unspecialized cell that can divide repeatedly and differentiate into specialized cells. Totipotent stem cells can form any cell type, including the placenta. Pluripotent stem cells can form any cell of the body. Multipotent stem cells can form a limited range of cell types, such as blood cells from bone marrow stem cells. A stem cell niche, such as the bone marrow, maintains stem cells and controls their division.

## Cell size and specialized cells
Cell size is limited because as a cell grows its surface area to volume ratio falls, so exchange of materials becomes too slow. Specialized cells include red blood cells, sperm and egg cells, alveolar cells and muscle fibres, each with structures suited to its function.

## Key terms
Differentiation: the process by which cells become specialized
Stem cell: an unspecialized cell that can divide and differentiate
Totipotent: able to form any cell type, including the placenta
Pluripotent: able to form any cell of the body
Multipotent: able to form a limited range of cell types
Morphogen: a signal whose concentration gradient controls development
Gas exchange:
# Gas exchange
## Gas exchange surfaces
Gas exchange is the diffusion of oxygen into an organism and of carbon dioxide out. Good gas exchange surfaces are permeable, thin, moist and large, and a concentration gradient is kept across them by ventilation and blood flow.

## Mammalian lungs
Air passes through the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles into the alveoli. The alveolus is a tiny air sac where gas exchange happens. Alveoli have walls one cell thick, are surrounded by capillaries and are coated with surfactant, which lowers surface tension and stops them collapsing. Ventilation is the movement of air in and out of the lungs. Inhalation happens when the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, increasing the volume of the thorax and lowering its pressure.
Tidal volume is the volume of air breathed in or out in a normal breath. Vital capacity is the largest volume that can be breathed out after the deepest breath in.

## Plants and haemoglobin
Leaves exchange gases through stomata, opened and closed by guard cells. Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves. Haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Foetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin. The Bohr shift is the lowered affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen at higher carbon dioxide concentrations, which helps it release oxygen in respiring tissues.

## Key terms
Alveolus: a tiny air sac in the lungs where gas exchange happens
Surfactant: a substance that reduces surface tension in the alveoli
Ventilation: the movement of air into and out of the lungs
Tidal volume: the volume of air in a normal breath
Vital capacity: the largest volume that can be exhaled after the deepest breath in
Stoma: a pore in a leaf controlled by guard cells
Bohr shift: the drop in haemoglobin’s oxygen affinity at high carbon dioxide
Transport:
# Transport
## Blood vessels
Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure and have thick walls with elastic and muscle tissue. Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure and have valves that stop backflow. Capillaries are vessels one cell thick where materials are exchanged between blood and tissues. Tissue fluid is fluid that leaks out of capillaries and bathes the cells.

## The heart and circulation
Mammals have a double circulation: blood passes through the heart twice on each circuit, once to the lungs and once to the rest of the body. The heart has four chambers, and the left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood round the whole body. The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with blood.

## Transport in plants
Xylem is the tissue that carries water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves. Water moves up the xylem in the transpiration stream: evaporation from leaves creates tension that pulls water up, helped by cohesion and adhesion. Phloem is the tissue that carries sugars and other organic compounds. Translocation is the movement of sugars in phloem from sources, such as leaves, to sinks, such as roots and fruits. Root pressure can push water up the xylem when transpiration is low.

## Key terms
Artery: a vessel carrying blood away from the heart at high pressure
Vein: a vessel carrying blood back to the heart, with valves
Capillary: a vessel one cell thick where exchange happens
Double circulation: blood passing through the heart twice per circuit
Xylem: the tissue carrying water and minerals
Phloem: the tissue carrying sugars and organic compounds
Translocation: the movement of sugars in phloem from source to sink
Transpiration: loss of water vapour from leaves
Muscle and motility:
# Muscle and motility
## Movement
Motility is the ability of an organism to move by itself. Sessile organisms stay in one place; motile organisms move to find food, escape predators or reproduce.

## Muscle contraction
Skeletal muscle is made of muscle fibres containing myofibrils. The sarcomere is the contractile unit of a myofibril, made of overlapping actin and myosin filaments. The sliding filament model states that muscle contracts when myosin heads bind to actin and pull it towards the centre of the sarcomere using energy from ATP, shortening the sarcomere. Calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum expose the binding sites on actin by moving tropomyosin. Titin is a protein that acts as a spring and helps the sarcomere return to its resting length.

## The skeleton and joints
Muscles work in antagonistic pairs because a muscle can only pull. A synovial joint, such as the hip or knee, has a capsule of synovial fluid that reduces friction. Tendons attach muscles to bones; ligaments attach bones to bones.

## Key terms
Sarcomere: the contractile unit of a myofibril
Actin: the thin filament of a sarcomere
Myosin: the thick filament whose heads pull actin
Sliding filament model: contraction by actin sliding over myosin
Antagonistic muscles: a pair of muscles with opposite actions
Synovial joint: a freely moving joint lubricated by synovial fluid
Tendon: tissue attaching muscle to bone
Adaptation to environment:
# Adaptation to environment
## Habitat and adaptation
A habitat is the place where a community, species, population or organism lives. An adaptation is a characteristic that suits an organism to its environment, produced by natural selection.

## Adaptations to extreme environments
Xerophytes are plants adapted to dry environments, with features such as thick waxy cuticles, sunken stomata, reduced leaves and CAM photosynthesis; marram grass and cacti are examples. Halophytes are plants adapted to salty environments, such as mangroves. Desert animals reduce water loss and avoid heat, for example by being active at night.

## Abiotic factors and biomes
Abiotic factors are non-living factors, such as temperature, light, water and soil pH, that limit where species can live. The range of tolerance is the range of an abiotic factor in which a species can survive. A biome is a group of ecosystems with similar climate and communities, such as tropical rainforest, hot desert, tundra and grassland. Hermatypic corals need warm, shallow, clear water.

## Key terms
Habitat: the place where an organism or species lives
Adaptation: a characteristic that suits an organism to its environment
Xerophyte: a plant adapted to dry conditions
Halophyte: a plant adapted to salty conditions
Range of tolerance: the range of an abiotic factor in which a species can survive
Biome: a group of ecosystems with similar climate and communities
Ecological niches:
# Ecological niches
## The niche
An ecological niche is the role of a species in an ecosystem, including its habitat, its interactions with other species and its use of resources. The fundamental niche is the range a species could potentially occupy; the realized niche is the range it actually occupies because of competition and other interactions.

## Modes of nutrition
Autotrophs make their own organic compounds from inorganic substances; photoautotrophs use light and chemoautotrophs use chemical energy. Heterotrophs obtain organic compounds from other organisms. Holozoic nutrition is ingesting food and digesting it internally. Saprotrophs digest dead matter externally and absorb the products. Mixotrophs, such as Euglena, can feed both autotrophically and heterotrophically.

## Competition and feeding
Competitive exclusion is the principle that two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche in the same place for long. Herbivores and plants show adaptations to each other, such as grinding teeth in herbivores and toxins and spines in plants. Predators have adaptations for catching prey, and prey have adaptations for avoiding predators.

## Key terms
Ecological niche: the role of a species in its ecosystem
Fundamental niche: the range a species could potentially occupy
Realized niche: the range a species actually occupies
Autotroph: an organism that makes its own organic compounds
Heterotroph: an organism that obtains organic compounds from others
Saprotroph: an organism that digests dead matter externally
Competitive exclusion: the principle that two species cannot share one niche for long
Enzymes and metabolism:
# Enzymes and metabolism
## Enzymes
Metabolism is the web of all the enzyme-catalysed reactions in a cell or organism. Anabolism is the building of larger molecules from smaller ones; catabolism is the breaking down of larger molecules. An enzyme is a globular protein that acts as a biological catalyst, speeding up reactions without being used up. The active site is the region of an enzyme where the substrate binds.
The induced-fit model states that the active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds. Enzymes lower the activation energy, the energy needed to start a reaction.

## Factors affecting enzyme activity
Enzyme activity increases with temperature up to an optimum, because molecules collide more often; above the optimum the enzyme denatures. Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Activity increases with substrate concentration until every active site is occupied.

## Inhibition and control
A competitive inhibitor binds to the active site and blocks the substrate. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the shape of the active site. End-product inhibition is when the final product of a pathway inhibits an enzyme near its start, controlling the rate of the pathway.

## Key terms
Metabolism: all the enzyme-catalysed reactions in an organism
Anabolism: building larger molecules from smaller ones
Catabolism: breaking larger molecules into smaller ones
Active site: the region of an enzyme where the substrate binds
Induced fit: the slight change in shape of the active site as the substrate binds
Activation energy: the energy needed to start a reaction
Competitive inhibitor: a molecule that blocks the active site
Non-competitive inhibitor: a molecule that binds elsewhere and changes the active site
End-product inhibition: a pathway’s product inhibiting an early enzyme
Cell respiration:
# Cell respiration
## ATP
ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the molecule that supplies energy for cell activities. Energy is released when ATP is hydrolysed to ADP and phosphate. Cell respiration is the controlled release of energy from organic compounds to produce ATP.

## Aerobic and anaerobic respiration
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases a large amount of ATP, with carbon dioxide and water as products. Anaerobic respiration releases a small amount of ATP without oxygen. In humans anaerobic respiration produces lactate; in yeast it produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

## Stages
Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules, with a small net gain of ATP and reduced NAD. In aerobic respiration pyruvate enters the mitochondrion, where the link reaction and the Krebs cycle release carbon dioxide and produce reduced NAD and FAD. Oxidative phosphorylation is the production of most ATP on the inner mitochondrial membrane: the electron transport chain pumps protons, and ATP synthase uses the proton gradient in chemiosmosis. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water.

## Key terms
ATP: the molecule that supplies energy for cell processes
Glycolysis: the splitting of glucose into pyruvate in the cytoplasm
Krebs cycle: the stage in the mitochondrial matrix that releases carbon dioxide and reduced coenzymes
Oxidative phosphorylation: ATP production using the electron transport chain
Chemiosmosis: ATP synthesis driven by a proton gradient through ATP synthase
Anaerobic respiration: respiration without oxygen
Photosynthesis:
# Photosynthesis
## The process
Photosynthesis is the process in which light energy is used to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. The word equation is carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs mainly red and blue light. An absorption spectrum shows which wavelengths a pigment absorbs; an action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength. Chromatography separates photosynthetic pigments.

## Limiting factors
A limiting factor is the factor in shortest supply that limits the rate of photosynthesis. The rate can be limited by light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration or temperature. Carbon dioxide enrichment experiments test how rising carbon dioxide levels will affect plant growth.

## Stages
The light-dependent reactions happen in the thylakoids: light excites electrons in photosystems, water is split by photolysis releasing oxygen, and ATP and reduced NADP are made. The light-independent reactions, the Calvin cycle, happen in the stroma: the enzyme rubisco fixes carbon dioxide onto RuBP, and ATP and reduced NADP convert the product into triose phosphate, which is used to make glucose and other carbohydrates.

## Key terms
Chlorophyll: the green pigment that absorbs light
Absorption spectrum: the wavelengths a pigment absorbs
Action spectrum: the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength
Limiting factor: the factor in shortest supply that limits the rate
Photolysis: the splitting of water by light
Calvin cycle: the light-independent reactions that fix carbon dioxide
Rubisco: the enzyme that fixes carbon dioxide onto RuBP
Chemical signalling:
# Chemical signalling
## Signalling molecules
Cells communicate using signalling molecules called ligands, which bind to specific receptors. Signals include hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines and calcium ions. Quorum sensing is signalling between bacteria that lets them respond together once their population is dense enough, as in bioluminescence in Vibrio fischeri.

## Receptors
Transmembrane receptors are proteins in the plasma membrane that bind hydrophilic signals such as peptide hormones. Intracellular receptors are inside the cell and bind hydrophobic signals such as steroid hormones, which cross the membrane and change gene expression.

## Signal transduction
Signal transduction is the chain of events inside a cell triggered when a signal binds to its receptor. G-protein-coupled receptors activate G proteins and second messengers such as cyclic AMP. Receptor tyrosine kinases, such as the insulin receptor, add phosphate groups to proteins. Epinephrine acts through a G-protein-coupled receptor; oestradiol acts through an intracellular receptor.

## Key terms
Ligand: a signalling molecule that binds to a receptor
Quorum sensing: bacterial signalling that depends on population density
Transmembrane receptor: a membrane protein that binds a signal outside the cell
Intracellular receptor: a receptor inside the cell for signals that cross the membrane
Signal transduction: the chain of events triggered inside a cell by a signal
Second messenger: a molecule inside the cell that relays a signal, such as cyclic AMP
Neural signalling:
# Neural signalling
## Neurons
A neuron is a cell that carries electrical impulses. Sensory neurons carry impulses from receptors, motor neurons carry them to effectors, and relay neurons connect neurons within the central nervous system. Myelin is a fatty sheath around some axons that speeds conduction by saltatory conduction between the nodes of Ranvier.

## The nerve impulse
The resting potential is the potential difference of about −70 mV across the membrane of a resting neuron, maintained by the sodium–potassium pump. An action potential is a rapid reversal of the membrane potential: sodium ions diffuse in (depolarization), then potassium ions diffuse out (repolarization). The threshold potential must be reached for an action potential to start.

## Synapses
A synapse is a junction between two neurons. When an impulse arrives, calcium ions enter, vesicles release a neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine by exocytosis, and it diffuses across the synaptic cleft to bind receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. Excitatory neurotransmitters cause depolarization; inhibitory ones cause hyperpolarization. Neonicotinoid pesticides block acetylcholine receptors in insects.

## Key terms
Neuron: a cell that carries electrical impulses
Myelin: a fatty sheath that speeds conduction
Resting potential: the potential difference across a resting neuron membrane, about −70 mV
Action potential: a rapid reversal of membrane potential
Depolarization: the membrane becoming less negative as sodium ions enter
Synapse: a junction between two neurons
Neurotransmitter: a chemical that carries a signal across a synapse
Integration of body systems:
# Integration of body systems
## Coordination
Integration is the coordination of the body systems so that the organism works as a whole. The nervous system coordinates fast, short-lived responses with electrical impulses; the endocrine system coordinates slower, longer-lasting responses with hormones carried in the blood.

## The brain and reflexes
The brain is the main integrating organ. The cerebellum coordinates skeletal muscle movement and balance. A reflex is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus. A reflex arc is the pathway from a receptor through sensory, relay and motor neurons to an effector, as in the pain withdrawal reflex.

## Hormones and rhythms
The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems by controlling the pituitary gland. Melatonin is secreted by the pineal gland and controls circadian rhythms such as the sleep cycle. Epinephrine prepares the body for vigorous activity. In plants, phototropism is growth towards light, controlled by the hormone auxin.

## Key terms
Integration: coordination of body systems so the organism works as a whole
Reflex: a rapid automatic response to a stimulus
Reflex arc: the neural pathway of a reflex
Cerebellum: the part of the brain that coordinates movement and balance
Melatonin: the hormone that controls circadian rhythms
Phototropism: growth of a plant towards light
Defence against disease:
# Defence against disease
## Pathogens and barriers
A pathogen is an organism or virus that causes disease. The skin and mucous membranes are the first barrier against pathogens. Blood clotting seals cuts: platelets release clotting factors that lead to fibrinogen being converted into fibrin, which forms a mesh.

## Innate and adaptive immunity
Phagocytes are white blood cells that engulf and digest pathogens by phagocytosis; this is part of innate immunity. Lymphocytes provide adaptive immunity. An antigen is a molecule that triggers an immune response. An antibody is a protein made by B lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen. Plasma cells secrete large amounts of antibody, and memory cells give long-term immunity.

## Vaccines, antibiotics and zoonoses
A vaccine contains antigens that make memory cells form without causing the disease. Herd immunity is the protection of a population when enough people are immune that a pathogen cannot spread. Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses, and resistance to them evolves by natural selection. HIV destroys helper T cells, weakening the immune system. A zoonosis is a disease that passes from animals to humans, such as COVID-19.

## Key terms
Pathogen: an organism or virus that causes disease
Phagocyte: a white blood cell that engulfs pathogens
Antigen: a molecule that triggers an immune response
Antibody: a protein that binds a specific antigen
Memory cell: a lymphocyte that gives long-term immunity
Vaccine: a preparation of antigens that produces immunity
Herd immunity: protection of a population when most of it is immune
Zoonosis: a disease passed from animals to humans
Populations and communities:
# Populations and communities
## Populations
A population is a group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time. Population size can be estimated by random quadrat sampling for sessile organisms and by capture–mark–recapture with the Lincoln index for motile animals. Carrying capacity is the largest population an environment can support. A population grows exponentially at first, then levels off in a sigmoid curve as limiting factors increase.

## Interactions in communities
A community is all the populations of different species living together in an area. Intraspecific competition is between members of the same species; interspecific competition is between different species. Mutualism is an interaction in which both species benefit, such as root nodules in legumes. Predation and herbivory are interactions in which one species feeds on another. Parasitism benefits the parasite and harms the host.

## Control of populations
Top-down control is the control of a population by its predators; bottom-up control is by the availability of resources. Allelopathy is the release of chemicals by plants that inhibit other plants. Invasive species can outcompete native species.

## Key terms
Population: organisms of one species in one area at one time
Carrying capacity: the largest population an environment can support
Community: all the populations of different species in an area
Intraspecific competition: competition within a species
Interspecific competition: competition between species
Mutualism: an interaction that benefits both species
Parasitism: an interaction that benefits one species and harms the host
Transfers of energy and matter:
# Transfers of energy and matter
## Ecosystems
An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with each other and their abiotic environment. Most ecosystems depend on sunlight as their initial energy source. Energy flows through ecosystems, while chemical elements are recycled.

## Food chains and energy loss
A food chain shows the transfer of energy from one organism to the next. A trophic level is the position of an organism in a food chain. Producers are autotrophs at the first trophic level; consumers are heterotrophs. Energy is lost between trophic levels as heat from respiration and in material that is not eaten or digested, so usually only about 10% passes on, which limits the length of food chains. A pyramid of energy shows the energy at each trophic level.

## Productivity and the carbon cycle
Gross primary production is the total energy fixed by producers; net primary production is what remains after their own respiration. Decomposers release nutrients from dead organic matter. In the carbon cycle, carbon moves between the atmosphere, organisms, oceans and fossil fuels through photosynthesis, respiration, combustion and dissolving. The Keeling curve shows atmospheric carbon dioxide rising, with a yearly fluctuation.

## Key terms
Ecosystem: a community and its abiotic environment
Trophic level: the position of an organism in a food chain
Producer: an autotroph at the first trophic level
Decomposer: an organism that breaks down dead matter
Gross primary production: the total energy fixed by producers
Net primary production: energy fixed by producers minus their respiration
DNA replication:
# DNA replication
## Semi-conservative replication
DNA replication is the copying of DNA before cell division. Replication is semi-conservative: each new molecule has one strand from the original and one new strand. Complementary base pairing makes each new strand an accurate copy.

## Enzymes in replication
Helicase is the enzyme that unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the new strand, following the template. DNA polymerase only adds nucleotides in the 5′ to 3′ direction, so one strand is made continuously (the leading strand) and the other in short Okazaki fragments (the lagging strand), which DNA ligase joins. Primase makes a short RNA primer that DNA polymerase extends.

## PCR and gel electrophoresis
The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) copies a section of DNA many times using cycles of heating and cooling and a heat-stable DNA polymerase, Taq polymerase. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size in an electric field, as used in DNA profiling and in testing for COVID-19.

## Key terms
Semi-conservative replication: each new DNA molecule keeping one original strand
Helicase: the enzyme that unwinds DNA
DNA polymerase: the enzyme that builds a new DNA strand
Okazaki fragment: a short section of the lagging strand
DNA ligase: the enzyme that joins DNA fragments
PCR: the polymerase chain reaction, which copies DNA many times
Gel electrophoresis: separating DNA fragments by size in an electric field
Protein synthesis:
# Protein synthesis
## Transcription
Transcription is the copying of a base sequence of DNA into messenger RNA (mRNA). RNA polymerase separates the DNA strands and builds mRNA by complementary base pairing with the template strand, using uracil in place of thymine. The coding strand has the same sequence as the mRNA, apart from thymine.

## Translation
Translation is the synthesis of a polypeptide from the information in mRNA. A codon is a sequence of three bases on mRNA that codes for one amino acid. Translation happens at ribosomes. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry specific amino acids and have an anticodon that is complementary to a codon. The ribosome joins amino acids with peptide bonds in the order set by the codons. The start codon AUG begins translation, and stop codons end it.

## The code and mutations
The genetic code is degenerate, meaning more than one codon can code for the same amino acid. A change of one base can change one amino acid, as in sickle cell anaemia, where a base substitution changes glutamic acid to valine in haemoglobin.

## Key terms
Transcription: copying DNA into mRNA
Translation: making a polypeptide from mRNA
Codon: three mRNA bases coding for one amino acid
Anticodon: three tRNA bases complementary to a codon
RNA polymerase: the enzyme that makes mRNA
Degenerate code: more than one codon coding for the same amino acid
Mutation and gene editing:
# Mutation and gene editing
## Mutations
A gene mutation is a change in the base sequence of a gene. A substitution replaces one base with another, an insertion adds bases and a deletion removes them. Insertions and deletions not in multiples of three cause frameshift mutations. Mutations can be caused by mutagens, such as radiation and some chemicals, and by errors in replication.

## Consequences
Most mutations are neutral or harmful and a few are beneficial. Mutations in body cells are not inherited but can cause cancer; mutations in germ cells can be passed to offspring. Mutation is the original source of genetic variation and so of evolution.

## Gene editing
Gene knockout is a technique that stops a gene working so that its function can be studied. CRISPR-Cas9 is a gene-editing tool in which a guide RNA directs the Cas9 enzyme to cut DNA at a specific sequence. Conserved sequences are sequences that stay almost the same across species because changes to them are harmful.

## Key terms
Gene mutation: a change in the base sequence of a gene
Substitution: replacing one base with another
Frameshift mutation: a shift in the reading frame from an insertion or deletion
Mutagen: something that causes mutations
Gene knockout: deactivating a gene to study its function
CRISPR-Cas9: a gene-editing tool that cuts DNA at a chosen sequence
Conserved sequence: a sequence that is almost the same across species
Cell and nuclear division:
# Cell and nuclear division
## Cell division
Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm. In animal cells it happens by a cleavage furrow; in plant cells a cell plate forms. Mitosis is nuclear division that produces two genetically identical nuclei, used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Meiosis is nuclear division that halves the chromosome number and produces genetically different haploid nuclei, used to make gametes.

## Mitosis
Before mitosis the DNA is replicated, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids. In prophase the chromosomes condense; in metaphase they line up at the equator; in anaphase sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles; in telophase nuclear membranes re-form. The mitotic index is the proportion of cells in a sample that are in mitosis.

## Meiosis and variation
In meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair and separate in the first division, and sister chromatids separate in the second. Crossing over and random orientation of homologous pairs produce genetic variation. Non-disjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate, which can cause conditions such as Down syndrome. Uncontrolled cell division causes tumours; oncogenes are mutated genes that can cause cancer.

## Key terms
Cytokinesis: division of the cytoplasm
Mitosis: nuclear division producing identical nuclei
Meiosis: nuclear division halving the chromosome number
Sister chromatids: the two identical copies of a replicated chromosome
Homologous chromosomes: a matching pair of chromosomes, one from each parent
Crossing over: exchange of DNA between homologous chromosomes
Non-disjunction: failure of chromosomes to separate
Mitotic index: the proportion of cells in mitosis
Gene expression:
# Gene expression
## Controlling gene expression
Gene expression is the process by which the information in a gene is used to make a product such as a protein. It can be regulated at transcription, after transcription and at translation. Transcription factors are proteins that bind to promoters or enhancers to increase or decrease transcription.

## Epigenetics
Epigenetics is the study of heritable changes in gene expression that do not change the base sequence. DNA methylation, adding methyl groups to DNA, usually reduces transcription. Histone modification changes how tightly DNA is wound and so how easily it can be transcribed. Epigenetic tags can be affected by environmental factors such as diet and stress, and some can be inherited.

## Evidence
The transcriptome is all the RNA transcribed in a cell; the proteome is all the proteins it makes. Cells in one organism share a genome but have different transcriptomes. Studies of identical twins show that epigenetic differences increase with age.

## Key terms
Gene expression: using a gene’s information to make a product
Transcription factor: a protein that controls transcription
Epigenetics: heritable changes in gene expression without base changes
DNA methylation: adding methyl groups to DNA, usually silencing genes
Transcriptome: all the RNA transcribed in a cell
Proteome: all the proteins made by a cell
Water potential:
# Water potential
## Water potential
Water potential is a measure of the tendency of water to move from one place to another, measured in kilopascals. Pure water at atmospheric pressure has a water potential of zero. Water moves by osmosis from a region of higher (less negative) water potential to one of lower (more negative) water potential.

## Components
Water potential is the sum of solute potential and pressure potential. Solute potential is always negative or zero, because dissolved solutes lower water potential. Pressure potential is usually positive in plant cells, where the cell wall pushes back on the cell contents.

## Plant cells in solutions
A hypotonic solution has a higher water potential than the cell, so water enters and a plant cell becomes turgid. A hypertonic solution has a lower water potential, so water leaves and the cell becomes plasmolysed as the membrane pulls away from the wall. Animal cells have no wall and can burst in pure water, so medical solutions are made isotonic.

## Key terms
Water potential: the tendency of water to move, in kilopascals
Solute potential: the part of water potential due to dissolved solutes, always negative or zero
Pressure potential: the part of water potential due to pressure
Turgid: swollen with water, pressing on the cell wall
Plasmolysis: the membrane pulling away from the cell wall as water leaves
Isotonic: having the same water potential
Reproduction:
# Reproduction
## Sexual and asexual reproduction
Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical offspring from one parent. Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of gametes and produces genetically varied offspring. Fertilization is the fusion of a male gamete and a female gamete to form a zygote.

## Human reproduction
Sperm are produced in the testes and eggs in the ovaries. The menstrual cycle is controlled by FSH, LH, oestradiol and progesterone: FSH stimulates follicle development, a surge of LH triggers ovulation, and progesterone maintains the lining of the uterus. In vitro fertilization (IVF) is fertilization outside the body, using hormones to stimulate the ovaries first.

## Plant reproduction
Flowers are the reproductive organs of flowering plants. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma, by insects, wind or other means. Cross-pollination between different plants increases variation, and self-incompatibility prevents self-pollination in many species. After fertilization the ovule develops into a seed and the ovary into a fruit, which helps disperse the seeds.

## Key terms
Fertilization: fusion of a male and a female gamete
Gamete: a haploid sex cell
Ovulation: release of an egg from an ovary
FSH: follicle-stimulating hormone, which stimulates follicle growth
LH: luteinizing hormone, whose surge triggers ovulation
Pollination: transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
Seed dispersal: spreading seeds away from the parent plant
Inheritance:
# Inheritance
## Genes and alleles
A gene is a heritable factor that controls a particular characteristic. An allele is one specific form of a gene. A genotype is the combination of alleles of an organism; a phenotype is its observable characteristics. Homozygous means having two identical alleles of a gene; heterozygous means having two different alleles.
A dominant allele is expressed in a heterozygote; a recessive allele is only expressed when homozygous. Codominant alleles are both expressed in a heterozygote, as in the ABO blood groups.

## Crosses
Mendel showed that the alleles of a gene separate into different gametes. A Punnett grid predicts the genotypes of offspring. A monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes gives a 3:1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes. A test cross with a homozygous recessive reveals an unknown genotype.

## Sex linkage and polygenic traits
Sex-linked genes are carried on the X chromosome, so recessive conditions such as haemophilia and red–green colour blindness are more common in males. A pedigree chart shows the inheritance of a condition in a family. Polygenic traits, such as height and skin colour, are controlled by many genes and show continuous variation. A chi-squared test checks whether observed ratios differ significantly from expected ones.

## Key terms
Gene: a heritable factor controlling a characteristic
Allele: one specific form of a gene
Genotype: the alleles an organism has
Phenotype: the observable characteristics of an organism
Dominant allele: an allele expressed in a heterozygote
Recessive allele: an allele expressed only when homozygous
Codominant alleles: alleles both expressed in a heterozygote
Sex linkage: inheritance of genes carried on the X chromosome
Homeostasis:
# Homeostasis
## Homeostasis and negative feedback
Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment within narrow limits. Negative feedback is a mechanism in which a change triggers a response that reverses it, returning a variable to its set point.

## Blood glucose
Blood glucose is controlled by the pancreas. When blood glucose rises, beta cells secrete insulin, which makes liver and muscle cells take in glucose and store it as glycogen. When blood glucose falls, alpha cells secrete glucagon, which makes the liver break glycogen down into glucose. Type 1 diabetes is caused by the destruction of beta cells; type 2 diabetes is caused by cells becoming resistant to insulin.

## Temperature and water balance
Body temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus. When the body is too hot, vasodilation and sweating increase heat loss; when it is too cold, vasoconstriction, shivering and brown adipose tissue reduce heat loss and generate heat. Osmoregulation is the control of the body's water and solute balance; the kidney changes how much water is reabsorbed under the control of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Excretion is the removal of waste products of metabolism, such as urea.

## Key terms
Homeostasis: keeping a constant internal environment
Negative feedback: a response that reverses a change
Insulin: the hormone that lowers blood glucose
Glucagon: the hormone that raises blood glucose
Vasodilation: widening of skin arterioles to lose heat
Osmoregulation: control of water and solute balance
ADH: antidiuretic hormone, which increases water reabsorption in the kidney
Natural selection:
# Natural selection
## The theory
Natural selection is the process by which individuals with characteristics better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more, so the alleles for those characteristics become more common. It depends on variation, overproduction of offspring, competition and the inheritance of characteristics. Variation comes from mutation, meiosis and sexual reproduction.

## Types of selection
Directional selection favours one extreme of a characteristic. Stabilizing selection favours the average and removes the extremes. Disruptive selection favours both extremes. Sexual selection is selection for characteristics that improve mating success, such as the tail of a peacock.

## Gene pools
A gene pool is all the genes and alleles in an interbreeding population. Evolution is a change in allele frequencies in a gene pool over time. The Hardy–Weinberg equation, p² + 2pq + q² = 1, predicts genotype frequencies in a population that is not evolving. Examples of natural selection include antibiotic resistance in bacteria and the guppies studied by John Endler.

## Key terms
Natural selection: better-adapted individuals surviving and reproducing more
Gene pool: all the alleles in an interbreeding population
Directional selection: selection favouring one extreme
Stabilizing selection: selection favouring the average
Disruptive selection: selection favouring both extremes
Sexual selection: selection for traits that improve mating success
Stability and change:
# Stability and change
## Stable ecosystems
A stable ecosystem is one that persists over long periods and recovers from disturbance. Stability depends on biodiversity, a steady supply of nutrients and the absence of extreme disturbance. A tipping point is a threshold beyond which an ecosystem changes rapidly to a different state, such as rainforest turning to savanna.

## Succession
Succession is the series of changes in a community over time. Primary succession starts on bare ground with no soil, beginning with pioneer species such as lichens. Secondary succession happens where soil remains after a disturbance such as a fire. The final stable community is the climax community.

## Human impacts and sustainability
A keystone species has a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem, such as wolves in Yellowstone. Sustainable use of a resource takes no more than can be replaced. Eutrophication is the excessive growth of algae caused by nutrient runoff, which lowers the oxygen in water. Biomagnification is the increasing concentration of a pollutant, such as mercury, at higher trophic levels.

## Key terms
Succession: a sequence of changes in a community over time
Primary succession: succession starting on bare ground without soil
Climax community: the stable community at the end of succession
Keystone species: a species with a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem
Tipping point: a threshold beyond which an ecosystem changes rapidly
Eutrophication: excess algal growth from nutrient runoff
Biomagnification: increasing pollutant concentration up a food chain
Climate change:
# Climate change
## The greenhouse effect
The greenhouse effect is the warming of the Earth's surface by atmospheric gases that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour. The enhanced greenhouse effect is the extra warming caused by human release of greenhouse gases, mainly from burning fossil fuels and deforestation.

## Effects of climate change
Climate change brings rising temperatures, melting ice, rising sea levels and more extreme weather. Positive feedback speeds up warming: melting permafrost releases methane, and melting ice lowers albedo. Phenology is the timing of seasonal events such as flowering and migration; climate change shifts it and can cause mismatches between species. The ranges of many species are shifting towards the poles and uphill. Ocean acidification is the fall in ocean pH as seawater absorbs carbon dioxide, which threatens coral reefs.

## Mitigation
Carbon sequestration is the removal and storage of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, for example by planting forests and restoring peat bogs. Cutting fossil fuel use and protecting ecosystems are the main ways to limit climate change.

## Key terms
Greenhouse effect: warming by gases that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation
Enhanced greenhouse effect: extra warming caused by human emissions
Positive feedback: a change that causes more of the same change
Phenology: the timing of seasonal biological events
Ocean acidification: falling ocean pH as seawater absorbs carbon dioxide
Carbon sequestration: capturing and storing atmospheric carbon dioxide
